title: Exact Asymptotic Rates and an Exponential Strong Converse for quantum SMP and One-Way Communication
abstract: Computing many instances jointly can reduce communication per instance. We ask whether such savings occur in the simultaneous-message-passing (SMP) model and how they depend on quantum messages and shared resources. For every finite total function $f$ and fixed error $0\le\varepsilon<1$, we prove that the optimal worst-case communication per instance for $f^n$ converges to \[ D^\parallel(f)=\log|\mathrm{Row}(f)|+\log|\mathrm{Col}(f)|, \] where $\mathrm{Row}(f)$ and $\mathrm{Col}(f)$ are the sets of distinct rows and columns of the table $(f(x,y))_{x,y}$. This holds for classical and quantum SMP without shared entanglement, with or without shared randomness. Thus, transmitting row and column indices is asymptotically optimal, even with bounded error, joint computation, and quantum messages. In particular, the exponential advantage of quantum fingerprinting for a single instance of equality without shared randomness disappears in the asymptotic rate. We also prove that the same threshold governs an exponential strong converse: every fixed worst-case communication rate below it forces the probability of computing all $n$ outputs correctly to decay as $2^{-Ω(n)}$, even on average under a fixed product input distribution. With shared randomness, the optimal expected communication rate is $(1-\varepsilon)D^\parallel(f)$. Entanglement shared between each sender and the referee halves both rates; arbitrary tripartite entanglement gives no further reduction. The results extend to a class of total relations and yield one-way characterizations with $D^\parallel(f)$ replaced by $\log|\mathrm{Row}(f)|$. Our proof reduces SMP to one-way communication and relates successful computation to sampling based on quantum min-entropy; we also give a simpler proof of the key lemma using the pretty-good measurement.
summary: This paper provides exact characterizations for the asymptotic communication rates in quantum Simultaneous-Message-Passing (SMP) and one-way communication models. It proves that the rate is governed by the structure of the function, $D^\parallel(f)$, and establishes an exponential strong converse for this rate. The work quantifies how shared quantum resources like entanglement affect these fundamental communication limits.
main_problem: The paper determines the exact asymptotic communication rate required to compute joint functions in the quantum Simultaneous-Message-Passing (SMP) model and establishes the corresponding exponential strong converse.
main_result: The optimal worst-case asymptotic rate is characterized by $D^\parallel(f) = \log|\mathrm{Row}(f)| + \log|\mathrm{Col}(f)|$, and the strong converse shows that rates below this threshold lead to exponentially decaying success probabilities.
method: The proof relates the SMP problem to one-way communication and utilizes techniques involving quantum min-entropy and the pretty-good measurement to establish bounds on the success probability.
model_or_system: The analysis focuses on quantum communication complexity protocols, specifically the SMP model and one-way communication, considering the effects of shared randomness and entanglement.
key_observables: Optimal asymptotic communication rate, success probability decay rate ($2^{-\Omega(n)}$), and the quantities $D^\parallel(f)$ and $\log|\mathrm{Row}(f)|$.
important_parameters: Error $\epsilon$, number of instances $n$, and the structure of the function $f$ (via its row/column sets).
main_assumptions: The results hold for total functions $f$ satisfying certain structural conditions (C.I) and (C.II).
paper_structure: The paper establishes the strong converse first, then derives the exact rates for worst-case and expected communication, quantifying the impact of shared entanglement and randomness.
why_interesting: While focused on communication complexity, the rigorous analysis of quantum information bounds, entropy, and the use of quantum measurements (like PGM) are fundamental theoretical tools applicable to understanding resource limitations in quantum many-body simulations or quantum networking protocols.
